reference.source: Green's Operative Hand Surgery / Campbell's Operative Orthopaedics
clinicalPearls: Presents with painful and progressive global restriction of glenohumeral movement affecting both active and passive range
Loss of passive external rotation is characteristic and helps distinguish it from rotator cuff and subacromial disorders
The illness classically evolves through three overlapping phases: a painful freezing phase, a stiff frozen phase and a gradual thawing phase of recovery
There is a strong association with diabetes mellitus, in whom the disease is often bilateral and more refractory, and with thyroid dysfunction
It is described as primary (idiopathic) or secondary to trauma, immobilisation or surgery
It most often affects people between about 40 and 60 years of age with a slight female predominance
Radiographs are typically normal and mainly serve to exclude osteoarthritis, calcific tendinitis or a locked dislocation, so the diagnosis is largely clinical

Generic management includes analgesia, physiotherapy and stretching, corticosteroid injection and capsular distension (hydrodilatation), with manipulation under anaesthesia or arthroscopic capsular release for refractory cases
reference.pathophysiology: Adhesive capsulitis involves inflammation followed by fibrosis and contracture of the glenohumeral joint capsule, particularly at the rotator interval and the coracohumeral ligament, with a resulting reduction in joint volume. Fibroblastic proliferation and myofibroblast-driven contracture, mediated by cytokines and growth factors, thicken and tighten the capsule so that movement becomes globally restricted. Diabetes mellitus and thyroid disease predispose to the condition, which is usually self-limiting but resolves only slowly over many months to years.
additionalDifferentials: Referred pain or malignancy affecting the shoulder girdle
additionalInvestigations: Clinical examination demonstrating global loss of active and passive movement, especially external rotation
Plain radiographs to exclude osteoarthritis, a locked dislocation or calcific tendinitis
Assessment for diabetes mellitus and thyroid dysfunction
Ultrasound to exclude coexisting rotator cuff pathology
MRI or arthrography showing a contracted capsule and reduced joint volume when the diagnosis is uncertain
redFlags: A history of trauma with a locked shoulder suggesting a missed posterior dislocation
Night pain with systemic features or a mass raising concern for malignancy
A neurological deficit suggesting a cervical or nerve lesion
Failure to improve or an atypical presentation warranting further imaging
reference.prognosis: The condition is generally self-limiting but recovery is slow, often taking one to three years; people with diabetes tend to have a more protracted course and some are left with residual stiffness.
pitfalls: Missing a posterior dislocation, which also restricts external rotation, by not obtaining an axillary view
Labelling any stiff shoulder as frozen without excluding osteoarthritis or cuff pathology
Overlooking associated diabetes or thyroid disease
Overly forceful manipulation risking fracture or soft-tissue injury
management: Provide analgesia and anti-inflammatory measures for pain control, particularly during the painful freezing phase
Offer intra-articular glenohumeral corticosteroid injection to reduce pain and capsular inflammation early in the disease
Institute structured physiotherapy with graded stretching and range-of-motion exercises, intensified as pain settles
Reassure regarding the generally self-limiting but protracted course and advise activity modification
Optimise glycaemic control in diabetes and treat coexisting thyroid dysfunction, which influence severity and recovery
Consider capsular hydrodilatation, manipulation under anaesthesia or arthroscopic capsular release for refractory stiffness
Refer to a shoulder specialist when pain or restriction fails to improve despite conservative measures
